title: Unreal conditionals and wishes
seoTitle: Turkish unreal conditionals and keşke (I wish)
intro: In [B1 unit 9](b1-u09-grammar) the conditional `-sA` imagined, wondered and set real conditions. This unit makes conditions **unreal**: *Zengin olsam dünyayı gezerdim* (If I were rich, I'd travel the world), *Bilseydim gelirdim* (If I had known, I'd have come). The same forms carry wishes with *keşke*, **even if** with *bile* and *dA*, and **whatever happens**: *Ne olursa olsun*.

sections.title: Zengin olsam: if I were rich

blocks.text: To talk about something that isn't true now, Turkish puts the conditional `-sA` ([B1 unit 9](gp-conditional-sa)) in the if-clause and the past aorist `-(I)rdI` in the main clause, the form of **used to** from [B1 unit 2](gp-used-to): *Zengin olsam dünyayı gezerdim* (If I were rich, I'd travel the world). Nobody needs to add **but I'm not**: the form says it.

blocks.title: *gitmek* in the main clause: I would go

blocks.text: **The if-clause.** Verbs take `-sA` straight on the stem, as in B1: *gitsem*, *okusam*, *yapmasam*. Nouns, adjectives, *var* and *yok* go through *olmak*: *zengin olsam* (if I were rich), *burada olsan* (if you were here), *param olsa* (if I had the money), *vaktin olmasa* (if you didn't have time).

blocks.caption: Real or unreal
head: Real: it may be so
Unreal: it isn't so
Meaning
rows: if I'm rich · if I were rich
if you're here · if you were here
if I have the money · if I had the money
if you don't have time · if you didn't have time

blocks.text: **Aorist or -(I)rdI?** B1 unit 9 paired `-sA` with the aorist: *Param olsa bu evi alırım*. That imagines a case the speaker can still picture happening. With `-(I)rdI` the case is plainly contrary to fact: *Param olsa bu evi alırdım* adds **but I don't have the money**. Both translate English **would**, and both are everyday Turkish; when the condition is clearly untrue, `-(I)rdI` is the natural choice.

**Other main clauses.** `-(I)rdI` combines with the forms you know: *gelemezdim* (I couldn't come), *gelebilirdim* (I could come), and *iyi olurdu* (it would be good): *Biraz dinlensen iyi olurdu* (It would be good if you rested a bit).

**If I were you.** *Senin yerinde olsam* (if I were in your place), or just *yerinde olsam*, is the everyday way to give advice: *Senin yerinde olsam o işi kabul ederdim*. *Sen olsan ne yapardın?*, literally **if it were you**, asks **what would you do?**

items.en: If I were rich, I'd travel the world.
If I had the money, I'd buy this house.
If you were here, I'd be so happy.
If I were you, I'd tell him.
What would you do in my place?
If I had wings, I'd fly to you.

blocks.text: *Zenginsem* is not **if I were rich**. `-(y)sA` on a noun or adjective is a real condition, **if I'm rich** (and maybe I am). For an unreal one, use *olmak*: *zengin olsam*. In the same way *varsa* is **if there is**, and *olsa* **if there were**.

English and French mark the if-clause as past: **if I were**, **si j'étais**. Turkish marks the main clause instead: *gezerdim* is also **I used to travel**. After a `-sA` clause it can only mean **I would travel**.

For a past that didn't happen, the if-clause adds the past of **to be**, `-(y)DI`, after `-sA`: *bil-se-y-di-m*, **if I had known**. The buffer y always appears, since `-sA` ends in a vowel, and the ending comes last, as in the compound tenses of [B1 unit 1](gp-di-compounds). In Turkish grammar this is the past of the conditional (*şart kipinin hikâyesi*).

rows.en: if he or she had come
if you had come (plural or polite)
if he or she hadn't come
if you hadn't come (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **They.** *Gelselerdi* is the usual form; *gelseydiler* is also heard.
**The question goes on the main verb**, as with every if-clause: *Bilseydin gelir miydin?* (Would you have come if you'd known?). The if-clause itself has no question form.

blocks.title: Question on the main verb: would I have come?

rows.en: Would he or she have come?
Would you have come? (plural or polite)

blocks.text: **The main clause** is usually `-(I)rdI`, the same form as in the first section, so *gelirdim* means both **I'd come** and **I'd have come**: the if-clause decides. `-(y)AcAktI` ([B1 unit 2](gp-future-in-past)) is also common and sounds a little more definite, as if the plan had been made: *Bilseydim gelecektim*. Ability works too: *Haber verseydin seni karşılayabilirdim* (If you'd let me know, I could have met you).

blocks.caption: Nouns, adjectives and *var* go through *olmak*
head: Word
If it had been so
Meaning
rows: if I had had the money
if there hadn't been any traffic

blocks.text: **Real or unreal past.** [B1 unit 9](gp-conditional-real) gave *geldiysen*, **if you came**, when the speaker doesn't know whether you did: *Geldiysen neden aramadın?* (If you came, why didn't you call?). *Gelseydin* says you didn't: *Gelseydin beni görürdün* (If you'd come, you'd have seen me).

items.en: If I had known, I'd have come.
If we had left early, we wouldn't have missed the train.
If you had told me, I'd have helped you.
If there hadn't been any traffic, we'd have arrived on time.
If I had known, I'd have picked you up at the airport.
Would you have come if you'd known?

blocks.title: Haberim olsaydı
blocks.text: *Haberim yok*, literally **I have no news**, is the everyday **I don't know about it**. From it come *Haberim olsaydı* (if I'd known) and *Haberin var mı?* (Did you know? Have you heard?).

In speech the plain `-sA` sometimes stands for `-sAydI` when the past is obvious: *Dün gelsen görürdün*. Write `-sAydI`: *Dün gelseydin görürdün*. And never follow `-sAydI` with the aorist: *Bilseydim gelirim* mixes a past that didn't happen with a present habit.

*Keşke* (I wish, if only) opens a wish that can't come true, or probably won't. Its verb takes the conditional: `-sA` for the present and the future, `-sAydI` for the past. *Keşke* usually comes first, but it can also close the sentence: *Gelseydin keşke*.

head: A wish about
Example
Meaning
rows: I wish it wouldn't rain tomorrow.
I wish I had studied more.
I wish I hadn't said that.

blocks.text: **Never with -DI.** *Keşke geldim* is wrong: a wish needs the conditional, *Keşke gelseydim*. Nouns and adjectives go through *olmak*, as in the first section: *Keşke zengin olsam*, *Keşke orada olsaydın*.
**Keşke on its own** is an answer: *Yarın tatil mi? — Keşke!* (Is tomorrow a holiday? — I wish!). With *ben de* it joins in: *Keşke ben de gelseydim* (I wish I'd come too).

**Umarım: real hopes.** For something that may well happen, use *umarım* (I hope), the aorist of *ummak* (to hope), with the verb's ordinary tense: *Umarım yarın hava güzel olur* (I hope the weather is nice tomorrow), *Umarım beğenirsin* (I hope you like it). *Keşke* carries doubt or regret; *umarım* simply hopes. To wish someone something, use *dilemek*: *Sana başarılar dilerim* (I wish you every success).

items.en: I wish you were here.
I wish I knew more languages.
I wish I'd believed you that day.
I wish I hadn't said that.
I hope we see each other soon.

blocks.text: English **I wish** shifts the tense back (**I wish I knew**, **I wish I had known**); Turkish marks the same contrast with `-sA` and `-sAydI`: *Keşke bilsem*, *Keşke bilseydim*. **I hope** shifts nothing in either language: *Umarım bilirsin*.

sections.title: Olsa bile, olsa da: even if

blocks.text: Add *bile* (even) or the particle *dA* after an if-clause and it becomes **even if**: *Yağmur yağsa bile gideceğiz* (Even if it rains, we'll go). *DA* is the one of *ben de* (me too): written apart, with two-way harmony. After `-sA` it is always *da* or *de*: *yağsa da*, *gelse de*.

**Which conditional?** Usually the plain `-sA`, for a case you imagine: *Çok çalışsan da bu işi bir günde bitiremezsin* (Even if you work hard, you can't finish this job in a day). For the past, `-sAydI`: *Bilseydim bile söylemezdim* (Even if I had known, I wouldn't have said). Real conditionals take them too: *Gelirse bile geç gelir* (Even if he comes, he'll come late).

items.en: Even if it rains, we'll go.

items.tr: Çok çalışsan da bu işi bir günde bitiremezsin.
items.seg: Çok çalış|sa|n da bu işi bir günde bitiremezsin.
items.en: Even if you work hard, you can't finish this job in a day.
Even if I had known, I wouldn't have said.
Even if it's expensive, I'm going to buy it.
Even if he comes, he'll be late.

blocks.text: **Whether or not.** Two `-sA dA` clauses, positive and negative, mean **whether … or not**: *Yağmur yağsa da yağmasa da gideceğiz* (Whether it rains or not, we're going), *Gelsen de gelmesen de* (whether you come or not).

**Bile or dA?** Both are everyday. *Bile* is a little stronger: **even if it came to that**. *Bile* never changes; *dA* follows harmony. You will meet both words outside the if-clause in [B2 unit 8](gp-bile).
*DA* is written apart: *gelse de*, never *gelsede*. Only the locative suffix `-DA` is attached to its word (*evde*).

*Bile* and *dA* with `-sA` imagine a case. For something that really happened, **although** and **despite**, Turkish uses `-DIğI hâlde` and `-mAsInA rağmen`: *Yağmur yağdığı hâlde gittik* (Although it was raining, we went). They come in [B2 unit 3](gp-digi-halde).

In [B1 unit 9](gp-conditional-questions) a question word with `-sA` gave **whatever, wherever**: *Ne istersen al* (Take whatever you want). Repeat the verb after it, in the imperative or the optative, and it means **no matter what, whoever, wherever**: *Ne olursa olsun* (whatever happens, no matter what), *Kim gelirse gelsin* (whoever comes).

rows.en: whatever you do; do as you like

blocks.text: The second verb takes each person's command or wish form: the optative for **I** and **we** ([A2 unit 7](gp-optative)), the imperative for the others ([A1 unit 12](gp-imperative), [A2 unit 7](gp-imperative-3rd)). The first verb is usually in the aorist conditional. For **they**, *yaparlarsa yapsınlar* (also *yaparsalar*).

**Two uses.** Against a result that won't change, it means **no matter what**: *Ne yaparsam yapayım, bu kapı açılmıyor* (Whatever I do, this door won't open). Said to someone, it leaves the choice to them, often with a shrug: *Ne yaparsan yap, bana fark etmez* (Do whatever you like, it's all the same to me).

Nouns and adjectives go through *olmak*: *Kim olursa olsun* (whoever it is), *Ne kadar pahalı olursa olsun* (however expensive it is). *Ne olursa olsun* also stands alone as **no matter what**: *Ne olursa olsun, yarın oradayım* (No matter what, I'll be there tomorrow).

items.en: Whatever happens, I'll wait for you.
Whoever comes, don't open the door.
Whatever he says, don't believe him.
Wherever you go, I'll find you.

items.tr: Ne kadar çalışırsam çalışayım, bu işi bitiremiyorum.
items.seg: Ne kadar çalış|ır|sa|m çalış|a|y|ım, bu işi bitiremiyorum.
items.en: However hard I work, I can't finish this job.

blocks.text: *Nereye istersen gideriz* (We'll go wherever you want, B1 unit 9) offers a choice. *Nereye gidersen git, seni bulurum* (Wherever you go, I'll find you) says the choice changes nothing. The doubled verb makes the difference.

summary: `-sA` in the if-clause and `-(I)rdI` in the main clause make an unreal present: *Zengin olsam dünyayı gezerdim*; nouns, adjectives and *var* go through *olmak*: *param olsa*, not *param varsa*.
*Senin yerinde olsam…* (if I were you) and *Sen olsan ne yapardın?* (what would you do?) are the everyday frames for advice.
`-sAydI` is the unreal past: *bilseydim, gelmeseydin, gelselerdi*; the main clause takes `-(I)rdI` or `-(y)AcAktI`, and the question goes there: *gelir miydin?*
*Keşke* + `-sA` wishes about now (*Keşke burada olsan*), + `-sAydI` regrets the past (*Keşke gelseydim*); never *keşke* + `-DI`. Real hopes take *umarım*.
`-sA bile` and `-sA dA` mean **even if**; *yağsa da yağmasa da* means **whether it rains or not**.
Question word + `-(I)rsA` + the same verb in the imperative or optative means **no matter what, whoever, wherever**: *Ne olursa olsun*, *Kim gelirse gelsin*, *Ne yaparsam yapayım*.
